To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
prenatal and current household environmental tobacco smoke exposures are associated with increased risks of respiratory health outcomes among children in Taiwan.

prenatal exposure showed the strongest effects on all respiratory outcomes, and current household ETS exposure showed significant effects on a wide range of respiratory outcomes, including wheeze, asthma, and bronchitics.
maternal smoking and household ETS exposures increase the risks of respiratory symptoms and diseases in children, especially early-onset asthma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of household ETS exposure on the prevalence of respiratory outcomes in Taiwanese schoolchildren.
the effects of prenatal and household environmental tobacco smoke exposure on respiratory health in children in Taiwan.
the effects of household ETS exposure on the prevalence of respiratory outcomes in a Taiwanese population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in utero ETS exposure is the most important risk factor for respiratory outcomes in childhood.
the effects of ECTS exposure on respiratory outcomes in children were significant and that in utero exposure had the most profound effect on the development of respiratory disease.

maternal smoking during the prenatal and early postnatal periods, paternal smoking during the postnatal period, and joint parental smoking are all associated with the increased risk of respiratory outcomes in children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risks of asthma, bronchitis, and wheeze are higher in children exposed to ETS in utero and in the household.
maternal smoking is the most important risk factor for asthma and wheeze in children, and that joint exposure to parental ETS is associated with early onset of asthma in children.
prenatal ETS exposure had the strongest effect on respiratory health in our children, followed by household ETS exposure, and then maternal smoking alone.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of parental smoking on childhood respiratory health are more complex than previously thought.
joint exposure to parental tobacco smoking is a risk factor of early-onset asthma.
joint exposure to parental ETS may have a stronger impact on respiratory outcomes than exposure to maternal smoking alone.
